title: Page Guide
intro: Short answers to common questions, each tied to a published KRIOS page and a named source. The Guide never answers from drafts. If a question is not sourced well enough yet, it says so and points you to the published film instead.

labels.BELIEF: what a community holds to be true

a: KRIOS makes short documentaries on Greek history, faith and family memory, for Greeks in Greece and everywhere else. It describes itself as the living story of Greek civilization, with five aims: preserve, teach, understand, connect, pass forward.

items.q: How does KRIOS decide what goes into a film?
a: KRIOS says that if a claim cannot be traced to a source, it does not go in the film, and when the evidence runs out, the film says so. It prefers the oldest source to the most famous one, using primary sources and named scholarship for historical claims, checked before recording and again on the finished film.

items.q: How does KRIOS keep history, tradition and belief apart?
a: KRIOS says it separates what is documented, what the Church teaches, what families practice, and where communities differ. In this Guide, answers about contested or inherited subjects carry the labels HISTORY, TRADITION, BELIEF or PRACTICE so you can see which kind of statement you are reading.

KRIOS says it uses real archives first, credited with their licence. Where no photograph exists, some everyday scenes are illustrated. Those are marked, as with the labelled illustration on the home page, and they never stand in for sacred or historical evidence.
read: Image credits for The Greeks Who Left

items.q: Who narrates the films, and are there captions?
a: KRIOS says every documentary today is narrated in a human voice, and that new films get English and Greek captions reviewed by people.

groups.title: Find something to watch or read

a: The newest film is The Greeks Who Left, and the Greece They Carried (9 minutes, released October 18, 2026, Living Roots), about families who left Greece and what they carried with them. The film before it, The Greek Dance That Wasn't Real… Until It Was (11 minutes, October 11, 2026), is about dance, memory and what makes a tradition survive.

Sacred Days are KRIOS films released on the day of a feast or name day, on faith, customs and the traditions families carry forward. The Sacred Days page lists a curated calendar of feast days and says the Saint Demetrios film premieres on YouTube on Monday, October 26, 2026, the feast day.
read: When is Saint Demetrios name day?

items.q: When is the feast of Saint Demetrios, the name day of Dimitris and Dimitra?
a: KRIOS's published page gives October 26 as the feast of Saint Demetrios on the calendar followed by the Church of Greece, celebrated that day by people named Dimitris, Dimitrios and Dimitra. It adds that churches on the Old Calendar celebrate 13 days later, on November 8 of the civil calendar. The page cites one source, Saint John's Monastery.
read: When is Saint Demetrios name day?
sources: Saint John's Monastery: Saint Demetrius the Myrrh-streamer

items.q: Where can I find older films, articles and answers?
a: The Films page lists every KRIOS film, newest first. The Articles, Q&A and Quizzes sections hold the earlier written material.
The Memory Room on the home page offers questions to ask someone in your family, taken from the film pages. The home page says nothing there is saved or sent.

items.q: Why did Greeks leave Greece between 1890 and 1914?
a: The Migration Policy Institute says the first wave of emigration was spurred by the economic crisis of 1893, after a rapid fall in the price of currants. From 1890 to 1914 almost a sixth of the population of Greece emigrated, mostly to the United States and Egypt.
read: Sources for The Greeks Who Left
sources: Migration Policy Institute: Greece, A History of Migration (Kasimis and Kassimi, 2004)

items.q: What was the second wave of Greek emigration?
a: According to the Migration Policy Institute, more than one million Greeks emigrated in a second wave, mainly between 1950 and 1974, to Western Europe, the United States, Canada and Australia. It also says almost half of the post-war emigrants had returned to Greece.
read: Sources for The Greeks Who Left
sources: Migration Policy Institute: Greece, A History of Migration (Kasimis and Kassimi, 2004)

items.q: How many Greeks reached the United States in the first wave?
a: This is still an open question on the film page. It notes that published histories give figures from about 430,000 to more than 600,000, so the film says only "hundreds of thousands". No single approved source settles the number, so the Guide does not give one.
read: Sources for The Greeks Who Left

items.q: Is there a Greek dance group in the Chicago area?
a: The Greek dance film names the Orpheus Hellenic Folklore Society. Its About page says its repertoire includes dances from every region of Greece, with an adult group of young adults from the Chicago area and a youth group for children aged 9 to 15, and that it shares them through performances, workshops and lectures.

items.q: Is Sirtaki an ancient Greek dance?
a: The Guide does not answer this one yet. The KRIOS film on Sirtaki relies on general references that have not yet been upgraded to scholarship, and the film page marks one popular story as interpretation, not established fact. Please watch the film and read its sources for the full picture.
read: The Greek Dance That Wasn't Real… Until It Was

items.q: Was Greek music censored under dictatorship?
a: The Guide does not answer this yet. The film discusses it, but the sources it lists are not yet approved scholarship, so the Guide does not repeat the claims. The film page lists them.

groups.title: If your question is not here

a: The Guide only answers from published pages with a named source, so some questions have no answer here. Try the Q&A pages and the film pages, which show their sources.
